title.en: The Prophecy of the Bearded Strangers from the East

region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦蒂希卡科約姆（馬尼）

texts.period: Prophecy current before 1517; recorded by Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688)

source.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II, on the prophecies of the Indian priests

summary.en: Chilam Balam, great priest of Tixcacayom, prophesied that in the end of the thirteenth age, at the city of Tancab, the sign of a God of the heights would come and the Cross would manifest itself to the world, shining from pole to pole. 'Your Father comes, you Ytzalanos; your brother comes, you Tantunites. Receive your bearded guests from the East, who come bringing the sign of God.' The priest had a stone cross made and set in the temple courts, calling it the true tree of the world.
summary.zh: 蒂希卡科約姆的大祭司奇拉姆·巴拉姆預言：第十三紀之末，於坦卡布之城，將有高處之神的記號來到，十字向全世界顯現，自極北至極南光芒大作。「你們的父親來了，伊察人啊；你們的兄弟來了，坦通人啊。迎接你們自東方而來、攜神之記號的鬚客。」祭司遂命人琢石十字，立於神廟庭院之中，稱之為世界的真樹。

sensitivity.note: Seventeenth-century colonial record of a Yucatec prophecy; paraphrase of the Spanish original.

passages.text: In the end of the thirteenth age, being in his puhanga of Ytza and the city named Tancab, there shall come the sign of a God who is in the heights, and the Cross shall manifest itself to the world, by which the orb was lighted. There will be a division among the wills when this sign is brought in the time to come. The priests, before they come within a league and a quarter, shall see the Cross which appears to them and dawns from pole to pole.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II, prophecy of Chilam Balam; not verbatim.

passages.text: The cult of the vain gods shall cease. Your Father comes, you Ytzalanos; and your brother comes, you Tantunites. Receive your bearded guests from the East, who come bringing the sign of God. God is one, and merciful. The time of our life comes. Do not fear the world. Let us raise his sign on high, raise it to adore and to see it: the Cross we must raise. In opposition to the lie it appears today, against the first tree of the world. This is the sign of a God of the heights; this the Ytzalanas adore.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo (1688), prophecy of Chilam Balam; not verbatim.

passages.text: Those who believe shall be lighted in the age to come. Behold if it imports you what I say, warns and charges your interpreter and master of credit, Balam by name; and with this I have finished saying what the true God commanded me, that the world may hear it. Soon after the coming of the Spaniards, the Indians, seeing how much reverence was paid to the Cross, held certain what their Prophet had told them.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo (1688); not verbatim.

texts.language: Seventeenth-century Spanish record of a Yucatec prophecy

narrative.en:
Cogolludo preserves, in his 1688 history, the fullest colonial version of the prophecy cycle that Yucatec tradition attached to the coming of the Spaniards. The great priest of Tixcacayom, Chilam Balam (the 'jaguar priest'), is made to speak in the first person of the end of the thirteenth age: the sign of a God of the heights will appear, the Cross will dawn 'from pole to pole', the cult of the vain gods will cease, and bearded guests from the East — the Ytzalanos' father, the Tantunites' brother — must be received with good will because they carry the sign of God. The priest commands that his people raise the sign on high and adore it, in opposition 'to the lie' and 'against the first tree of the world' — a striking formulation in which the new cross displaces the old world-tree as the true axis of the world.

The historic kernel the chronicler gives is the episode of the woven mantle: before the strangers arrived, the prophet had a tribute-mantle woven in the pattern that the new tribute would take, and had it offered to the idols for safekeeping; he also had a cross made of stone and set in the courts of the temples, saying that this was the true tree of the world and that many peoples would come to venerate it. When Montejo entered Yucatán and the Indians saw the reverence paid to the Cross, they 'held certain what their Prophet had told them.'

Cogolludo reports several such prophecies from different priests (one from Ah Na Puc Tun about the last age purified by fire), and argues — with theological ingenuity — that the gift of true prophecy might have been given even to gentile priests, citing the example of Balaam: the prophetic word does not justify the prophet but serves the people who must hear it. As a corpus record this is the Maya 'return of the culture hero' motif transposed into colonial eschatology: the bearded god of the east whom the codices called Kukulcan reappears as the expected bearded strangers, and the prophecy becomes the ritual script with which the Maya of Yucatán narrated the catastrophe that overtook them.

The comparative value of the episode lies in its double framing. Read from within, it is a Maya prophecy: a priest foresees the foreigners, commands the reception of their sign, and orders a woven mantle as the pattern of the tribute to come. Read from without, it is a missionary construction: Cogolludo selects, translates, and theologically glosses the material to show that God announced the Gospel to the Indians through their own priests, citing Balaam as his warrant. Both readings are true, and the corpus record keeps both. For the Motif Atlas the record is the Maya contribution to the return-of-the-god cluster: the culture hero who promised to come from the east - Kukulcan, the bearded lord - is the figure whose return the bearded strangers are made to fulfill, in a colonial mirror image of the Popol Wuj expectation of the true dawn.

functions: Colonial-era eschatology: the conquest narrated as the fulfillment of a native prophecy
Explains the stone crosses found in Yucatec temple courts as pre-Christian tokens
Authorizes submission to the conquerors as obedience to the prophetic word

variants.name: Chilam Balam of Chumayel, katun prophecies
variants.text_tradition: Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel (Roys 1933)
variants.summary: The same expectation in katun form: '11 Ahau is the beginning of the count... the foreigners arrived from the east.'

primary_sources.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan

secondary_sources.citation: Tozzer, 1941, Cambridge: Peabody Museum (notes on the prophecies)

texts.sensitivity_guidance: The prophecy text is mediated by a missionary author arguing for conversion; note the colonial frame rather than presenting it as unmediated Maya voice.

title.en: Ah Na Puc Tun: The World Purified by Fire
title.zh: 阿·納·普克·圖恩：以火淨世

texts.period: Prophecy current before the Spanish arrival; recorded by Cogolludo 1688

source.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II

summary.en: Another gentile priest, called Ah Na Puc Tun, made the subjection to the Law of Grace notorious by his mouth, saying: In the last age, according to this reckoning, the cult of the vain gods will end, and the world will be purified with fire. He who sees it and weeps his sins with sorrow shall be called blessed.
summary.zh: 另有一位名阿·納·普克·圖恩的異教祭司，以其口使臣服於恩典之法一事昭然，他說：在最後的紀元，虛妄諸神的崇拜將終止，世界將以火淨化。凡見此事而含淚痛悔其罪者，有福了。

sensitivity.note: Seventeenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of the Spanish original.

passages.text: Notoria la hizo por la boca de otro Gentil Sacerdote, llamado Ah Na Puc Tun, que dijo: En la última edad, según esta determinación, habrá fin el culto de Dioses vanos, y el mundo será purificado con fuego. El que esto viere, y será llamado bienaventurado, si con dolor llorare sus pecados.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II; not verbatim.

passages.text: The antiquity of this priest has not been made out, but he appears to have flourished before the coming of the Spaniards, since he speaks of the last age; and by age they understood the space of time of twenty years. With the introduction of our Holy Catholic Faith the cult of the idols ceased, at least publicly, and this new world was purified with the fire of the Holy Spirit.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo (1688); not verbatim.

title.en: The Stone Cross: The True Tree of the World

source.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II

summary.en: The prophet commanded that a cross be made of stone and set in the courts of the temples, saying that this was the true tree of the world, and that many peoples would come to see it and venerate it from that time — the reason why, when the Spaniards asked them, the Indians said they went toward where the sun was born.
summary.zh: 先知命人琢石為十字，立於諸神廟庭院之中，說此乃世界的真樹，自此而後將有許多人民來見它、敬它——這也是西班牙人問路時，土人答以「往日出之地去」的緣故。

sensitivity.note: Seventeenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of the Spanish original.

passages.text: He commanded the lord of Mani, who was called Mochan Xiu, to offer that mantle to the idols, that it might be kept; and the sign of the Cross he had made of stone, and set it in the courts of the temples, where it was usually seen, saying that this was the true tree of the world, and that for this many peoples would come to see it and venerate it from that time.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo (1688), lib. II; not verbatim.

title.en: The Mantle of Tribute Woven as a Prophecy

source.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II

summary.en: The prophet had a mantle of tribute woven, and said that in that manner the tribute was going to be paid to those people; and he commanded the lord of Mani to offer the mantle to the idols, that it might be kept — a woven prophecy deposited in the temple, to be read against the tribute lists of the conquerors.
summary.zh: 先知命人織一貢賦披毯，並說：這些人的貢賦，就要照這式樣繳納；又命馬尼之君將此毯獻於神像之前，妥為收藏——一張織入廟中的預言，將與征服者的貢冊相對而讀。

sensitivity.note: Seventeenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of the Spanish original.

passages.text: Hizo texer una manta de tributo, y dixo, que de aquella manera havia de ser el tributo que se avia de pagar a aquellas gentes: y mando al Señor de Mani, que se llamaba Mochan Xiu, que se la ofreciese a los Idolos, para que estuviese guardada.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo (1688), lib. II; not verbatim.

title.en: Nacom Balam of Conil, the Old Man Who Received Montejo
title.zh: 科尼爾的納科姆·巴拉姆：接待蒙特霍的老人

region.zh: 墨西哥猶加敦海岸科尼爾

source.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II

summary.en: They came to a place called Coni, where there was only a rancho, where an old man lived, called Nacom Balam, who afterwards was named Pedro, because this was the name of the principal Spaniard. The Indians did not determine at once to take up arms against the Spaniards, but provided themselves, waiting what would befall with them.
summary.zh: 他們行至一處名科尼之地，那裡只有一座棚屋，住著一位老人，名納科姆·巴拉姆，後來改名佩德羅，因這是那位西班牙首要人物的名字。印第安人並未即刻舉兵，而是各自治備，靜觀其變。

sensitivity.note: Seventeenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of the Spanish original.

passages.text: They were going from pueblo to pueblo until they reached one called Conil. It was not called Conil but Coni, because Conil is another seaport; and there was only a rancho, where an old man lived, called Nacom Balam, who afterwards was named Pedro, because this was the name of the principal Spaniard.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo (1688), lib. II; not verbatim.

title.en: The Eaters of Anonas: Indians Naming the Spaniards
title.zh: 食番荔枝者：土人為西班牙人命名

source.work: Diego Lopez de Cogolludo, Historia de Yucathan (1688), lib. II

summary.en: They went to the pueblo of Coba, now depopulated, and there it was that the Spaniards were called by the Indians in their language Ah makal kopob, which means the eaters of anonas, a fruit of that land; the Indians, amazed, watched them eat the fruit without considering whether it was noxious or not.
summary.zh: 他們行至科巴村（今已荒蕪）；正是在那裡，西班牙人被土人以土語稱為「阿·馬卡爾·科波布」——食番荔枝者，番荔枝乃當地果物。土人驚異地看他們吃這果子，全然不問其是否有毒。

sensitivity.note: Seventeenth-century colonial record; paraphrase of the Spanish original.

passages.text: They passed to the pueblo of Coba, now depopulated, and there it was that the Spaniards were called by the Indians in their language Ah makal kopob, which means the eaters of anonas, which is a fruit of that land: the Indians were amazed to see them eat them without considering whether they were noxious or not.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Cogolludo (1688), lib. II; not verbatim.
